title: Иерархическая модель структуры документа для решения задачи генерации конспектов лекций
abstract: В статье предлагается модель описания структуры документа, основанная на методах анализа иерархической структуры документа (HDSA) и формализме теории графов. В рамках предложенного подхода документ рассматривается как иерархическая система взаимосвязанных структурных элементов, включающая заголовки различных уровней, текстовые блоки, таблицы, формулы, изображения и иные типы контента. Каждый элемент интерпретируется, как вершина графа, а отношения вложенности и логической зависимости между элементами описываются с использованием ориентированных ребер графовой структуры. Применение предложенной модели к корпусу документов из различных предметных областей позволило выявить устойчивые закономерности организации текстового материала, характерные для конкретных типов документов. На основе полученных характеристик был сформирован набор JSON-шаблонов, описывающих типовые структуры документов для различных предметных областей, включая технические, юридические и научно-образовательные материалы. Каждый шаблон содержит формализованное описание структуры документа, включая допустимые уровни заголовков, ограничения на типы содержимого, а также параметры стилевого и композиционного оформления. Дополнительно шаблон может включать сведения о предпочтительном формате представления данных, правилах генерации таблиц, формул и специализированных текстовых конструкций. Использование JSON-формата обеспечивает машинно-ориентированное представление структуры документа и возможность интеграции шаблонов в программные системы автоматической генерации текста. Разработанные шаблоны предназначены для использования в процессе генерации текстов большими языковыми моделями (Large Language Models – LLM). В рамках предложенного подхода шаблон выступает как формализованное структурное ограничение, определяющее допустимую организацию итогового документа и последовательность формирования его разделов. Это позволяет снизить вариативность структуры генерируемого текста, повысить согласованность взаимосвязанных разделов и обеспечить соответствие результата требованиям конкретной предметной области. Предложенный подход ориентирован на реализацию управляемой генерации документов, при которой большая языковая модель выполняет генерацию содержимого в рамках заранее заданной структурной схемы. За счет этого обеспечивается более стабильное качество формирования документа, уменьшается вероятность нарушения логики построения текста и повышается воспроизводимость результатов генерации. Кроме того, использование структурных шаблонов позволяет адаптировать процесс генерации под различные типы документов без изменения архитектуры самой языковой модели. This article proposes a document structure description model based on Hierarchical Document Structure Analysis (HDSA) methods and the formalism of graph theory. Within the proposed approach, a document is considered as a hierarchical system of interconnected structural elements, including headings of different levels, text blocks, tables, formulas, images, and other types of content. Each element is interpreted as a graph vertex, while nesting and logical dependency relationships between elements are described using directed edges of the graph structure. The application of the proposed model to a corpus of documents from various subject areas made it possible to identify stable patterns in the organization of textual material characteristic of specific document types. Based on the obtained characteristics, a set of JSON templates was developed to describe typical document structures for different subject areas, including technical, legal, and scientific and educational materials. Each template contains a formalized description of the document structure, including permissible heading levels, constraints on content types, and parameters of stylistic and compositional formatting. Additionally, a template may include information on the preferred data presentation format, rules for generating tables and formulas, and specialized textual constructions. The use of the JSON format provides a machine-oriented representation of the document structure and enables the integration of templates into software systems for automatic text generation. The developed templates are intended for use in text generation by large language models (LLMs). Within the proposed approach, a template serves as a formalized structural constraint that defines the permissible organization of the resulting document and the sequence in which its sections are generated. This makes it possible to reduce the structural variability of generated text, improve the consistency of interrelated sections, and ensure that the resulting document complies with the requirements of a specific subject area. The proposed approach is aimed at implementing controlled document generation, in which a large language model generates content within a predefined structural scheme. This provides more stable document generation quality, reduces the likelihood of violations in the logical organization of the text, and improves the reproducibility of generation results. Furthermore, the use of structural templates makes it possible to adapt the generation process to different document types without modifying the architecture of the language model itself.

title: Industrial IoT Control Systems Using Fuzzy Logic
abstract: The rapidly developing field of control systems for the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), with a particular emphasis on the functioning of fuzzy logic. The purpose of this work is to investigate the current developments and problems in the application of fuzzy logic to improve the efficiency and rigidity of control systems in artificial environments. It does this by conducting an exhaustive assessment of recent research and case studies, which outlines the benefits and drawbacks of fuzzy logic in terms of optimizing control systems for the Internet of Things domain. As an additional point of interest, the abstract draws attention to the emerging investigation directions and unresolved difficulties that will influence the future of this field. This work contributes to the continuing conversation about the use of fuzzy logic for advanced control results in artificial Internet of Things environments by synthesizing existing knowledge and identifying gaps in understanding.

title: Learning-Theoretic Foundation for General Coded Computing: The Straggler Setting
abstract: Coded computing has emerged as a powerful paradigm for mitigating the impact of straggling workers in distributed computing systems. However, existing coded-computing schemes are predominantly designed for the exact recovery of highly structured computations, such as polynomial evaluation and matrix multiplication, and typically rely on strict recovery thresholds. These assumptions significantly limit their applicability to modern machine-learning workloads, particularly deep neural networks (DNNs), whose computations generally lack rigid algebraic structure and, in many applications, require only accurate approximations rather than exact recovery. To address this gap, we revisit coded computing from a learning-theoretic perspective and introduce General Coded Computing (GCC). Rather than adopting existing algebraic tools, GCC formulates coded computing through a natural end-to-end mean-squared error loss that directly measures the discrepancy between the desired computations and their recovered estimates. By deriving suitable upper bounds and restricting the encoder and decoder to a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) with mild smoothness constraints, we show that both the encoder and decoder admit specific representations as linear combinations of RKHS kernel functions. This representation allows the corresponding coefficients to be computed efficiently. Moreover, this framework enables us to establish theoretical performance guarantees for GCC under two complementary straggler regimes. In the worst-case setting with $N$ worker nodes, and at most $S$ stragglers, we show that the end-to-end loss decays at least at rate $O(S^3N^{-3})$ for standard configurations. We then study a probabilistic setting in which each worker independently straggles with probability $p$. We prove that the expected loss can still converge at rate $O(\log_{1/p}^3(N)N^{-3})$.

title: A Formal Limitation on Learning Human Language From Textual Corpora
abstract: Can a listener recover what a speaker means from the form of an utterance alone? We answer this question information-theoretically, and for a listener given by any featurizer of text, including the hidden states of contemporary large language models. Modeling language use as a joint distribution over meanings, contexts, and utterances, we derive upper bounds on the probability that a decoder recovers a speaker's intended meaning from a representation of the utterance. The bounds are governed by the uncertainty that form leaves about meaning, which splits into an irreducible part and a part that only (extralinguistic) context, but never the utterance alone, can resolve. Because these quantities are intrinsic to language, no representation, however much text or supervision produced it, can surpass them. The bounds apply, moreover, to meaning spaces that are discrete or continuous. We provide empirical evidence in support of the theory through experiments on artificial languages, Mandarin zero-pronoun resolution, and color reference.

title: Hardware-Efficient Error Mitigation and Shot-Efficient Sampling on IBM Quantum Hardware
abstract: We experimentally study error mitigation and finite-shot sampling on superconducting quantum hardware under a constrained execution budget. The study combines calibration-aware qubit selection, circuit-depth scaling, zero-noise extrapolation, dynamical decoupling, readout-error mitigation, and repeated-shot estimation on an IBM Quantum processor. Experiments are organized across ideal simulation, noise-model simulation, and physical-device execution to separate sampling uncertainty from device-induced error. We investigate how mitigation performance changes with circuit depth, effective noise scale, qubit connectivity, and measurement budget, and quantify accuracy using expectation-value error, mean-squared error, statistical uncertainty, and mitigation gain. A fixed hardware-execution budget is used to evaluate shot allocation strategies and repeated measurements without relying on unlimited sampling. The resulting analysis provides a hardware-aware characterization of when mitigation improves expectation-value estimation and when finite-shot fluctuations offset the benefit of additional mitigation overhead. The implementation uses contemporary Qiskit and IBM Quantum Runtime workflows and is designed to provide reproducible experimental evidence for error-mitigation studies on current quantum processors.

title: Solis666/cose-methodology: Capability-Oriented Software Engineering (COSE) — v1.0.0
abstract: Capability-Oriented Software Engineering (COSE) v1.0.0 Initial Public Release This release establishes the first public version of the Capability-Oriented Software Engineering (COSE) methodology. COSE is a software engineering methodology centered on the identification, formalization, composition, reuse, and evolution of software capabilities as primary engineering units. Included in this release Formal documentation of the COSE methodology Core concepts and terminology Methodological principles Capability-oriented architectural concepts Documentation of the methodology's development and rationale Reference material for applying COSE in software engineering contexts Relationship to the research paper This repository provides the public, evolving documentation of the COSE methodology. The formal research paper describing the methodology is published separately through Zenodo and constitutes the corresponding academic publication. This release represents the initial public version of the methodology documentation associated with COSE v1.0. Scope This release contains the methodology and its documentation. It does not constitute a release of a specific software implementation. Software systems developed using COSE may be published separately as implementations, demonstrations, or case studies. Version COSE Methodology: v1.0.0 Release type: Initial public release Full Changelog: https://github.com/Solis666/cose-methodology/commits/v1.0.0

title: Quantum-secure Software Network Environments for Telco Operators
abstract: The transition towards quantum-safe secure communications requires current network infrastructures to support the coexistence of multiple cryptographic technologies. In this context, crypto-agility becomes a key requirement, enabling the coordinated use of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), PostQuantum Cryptography (PQC), and classical cryptographic mechanisms during a progressive migration process. This paper presents a general, standards-based architecture for crypto-agile IPsec service provisioning in Software-Defined Networking (SDN) environments. The proposal combines modular functional blocks that support the integration of QKD-, PQC-, and classical-derived key material under a common operational framework. The architecture builds on existing specifications, including RFC 9061 and ETSI GS QKD 004. Rather thanfocusing on implementation details or performance evaluation, this work describes the needs addressed by the architecture, its main components, and the operational workflows supporting secure tunnel establishment, rekeying, and attestation-related actions.

title: Based on Neural Systems Dynamic Knowledge Graph Reasoning Engine
abstract: This paper presents a novel dynamic knowledge graph reasoning engine based on neural systems, aiming to enhance and infer from symbolic knowledge graphs more flexibly and explainably than traditional methods. The engine adopts a multi-module architecture comprising a neural enhancement module, a neural symbolic reasoning module, and an explainability module. The neural enhancement module, utilizing a Transformer architecture, learns and strengthens node and relation embeddings within the knowledge graph, capturing contextual dependencies and resolving ambiguities. The neural symbolic reasoning module, built upon graph neural networks, performs relation derivation based on the enhanced embeddings. Finally, the explainability module generates visualizations of the reasoning paths and provides probabilistic evidence support, facilitating user understanding of the reasoning process. This approach addresses the limitations of existing knowledge graph reasoning methods by integrating neural networks with symbolic knowledge, enabling dynamic graph enhancement and more interpretable reasoning for complex, uncertain, and context-sensitive knowledge inference problems. ---

title: Dynamic Quantum Network Resource Allocation Optimization
abstract: This paper addresses the critical challenge of optimizing resource allocation within dynamic quantum networks (QNs). The inherent complexities of QNs, including fluctuating demands, evolving topologies, and the fragility of quantum states, necessitate adaptive resource management strategies. We propose a novel algorithm leveraging reinforcement learning (RL) to dynamically adjust resource allocation based on real-time network conditions. The algorithm learns an optimal policy by iteratively interacting with a simulated QN environment, maximizing the overall quantum channel throughput while minimizing the probability of quantum error. Specifically, the core mechanism involves formulating the resource allocation problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), where the state represents the network's current configuration, the action represents the allocation of quantum resources (e.g., qubits, entanglement), and the reward reflects the successful completion of quantum communication tasks. The RL agent utilizes a Q-learning algorithm to estimate the optimal Q-function, guiding the allocation process. We demonstrate, through simulation, that our algorithm significantly outperforms static allocation strategies in terms of throughput and reliability, even under highly dynamic network conditions. The key contributions of this work lie in the integration of RL with the unique characteristics of QNs and the development of a practical algorithm for adaptive resource management. Further research will explore the scalability of this approach and its application to larger, more complex QN topologies.

title: Symbolic Regression with Neural Turing Networks for Discovering Mathematical Equations
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to mathematical equation discovery using Neural Turing Networks (NTNs) and symbolic regression. Traditional symbolic regression techniques often struggle with complex equations and require significant human intervention. We propose a system where an NTN iteratively refines a symbolic expression based on input data, effectively learning to generate mathematical equations. The NTN's memory capabilities are crucial for storing and retrieving relevant information, enabling the discovery of intricate relationships. We detail the architecture of the system, the training methodology, and present preliminary results demonstrating the potential of this combined approach. The core claim is that NTNs, while capable of mapping inputs to outputs, face challenges in directly discovering mathematical equations. We address this through a mechanism that utilizes an NTN to iteratively refine a symbolic expression, leveraging its memory to uncover complex mathematical relationships. This work represents a new integration of neural networks and symbolic regression, offering a potentially more automated and effective method for equation discovery.

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Graph Clustering
abstract: This paper investigates the inherent limits of graph clustering from an information-theoretic perspective. We argue that graph clustering fundamentally relies on compressing information regarding node relationships and propose that the information-theoretic limit provides a quantifiable measure of this redundancy. We derive a theoretical bound on achievable compression rates, leveraging concepts of mutual information and entropy, which is directly influenced by the graph's connectivity and node features. This work establishes a new framework for understanding graph clustering, offering a fundamental limit on clustering performance that can be used to evaluate and optimize clustering algorithms. The key contribution lies in shifting the focus from heuristic optimization to a rigorously defined, information-constrained objective.

title: Hierarchical Graph Embeddings with Relational Reasoning
abstract: Graph embeddings have emerged as a powerful technique for representing graphs in a continuous vector space, enabling applications like node classification, link prediction, and graph clustering. However, many existing graph embedding methods struggle to effectively capture the intricate and hierarchical relationships inherent within complex graphs. This paper introduces a novel hierarchical graph embedding approach that addresses this limitation by learning embeddings at multiple levels of granularity. The core of our method lies in a learned graph grammar that defines rules for transforming and combining embeddings, thereby explicitly modeling relational dependencies. We posit that by incorporating relational reasoning through this grammar, we can achieve a more nuanced and comprehensive representation of graph data compared to traditional, single-level embeddings. This approach allows for a richer understanding of graph structure and improves performance in downstream graph-related tasks. The method is described in detail, including the formulation of the learning objective, the design of the learned graph grammar, and the overall architecture of the embedding process.

title: Edge-Deployable Multi-Class Surveillance Video Anomaly Classification Using a MobileNetV2–LSTM Spatial–Temporal Framework
abstract: Automated surveillance systems require models that can recognize abnormal events accurately while maintaining efficient inference on resource-constrained hardware. This study proposes a lightweight spatial–temporal classification framework that integrates MobileNetV2 and Long Short-Term Memory networks for identifying five surveillance activity classes: Normal, Fighting, Burglary, Road Accident, and Explosion. Surveillance videos were preprocessed through frame sampling, resizing, normalization, and fixed-length sequence construction. MobileNetV2 was employed to extract compact frame-level spatial features, while the LSTM modeled temporal dependencies across consecutive frames. The framework was evaluated using accuracy, class-wise precision, recall, F1-score, macro F1-score, weighted F1-score, confusion-matrix analysis, and probability-based anomaly scoring. Experimental results on 463 video sequences show that the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 97.41%, a macro F1-score of 0.9612, and a weighted F1-score of 0.9744. Most classification errors occurred between visually similar human-centered anomaly classes, particularly Fighting and Burglary, while Normal and Explosion sequences were recognized with very high reliability. The trained model was converted into TensorFlow Lite format and deployed on a Raspberry Pi 4, achieving approximately 6–8 frames per second with an average latency of 120–150 ms per frame. These findings indicate that the proposed MobileNetV2–LSTM framework provides an effective balance between multi-class event recognition, temporal representation learning, and near-real-time edge inference. However, further validation on larger and more diverse surveillance datasets is required to confirm its generalizability under unconstrained operational conditions.

title: Closing the Loop in AI-Driven Biomedical Discovery
abstract: AI scientists generate hypotheses, propose experiments, and analyze datasets, and several have produced findings that were confirmed in the laboratory. Although they are opening a path to autonomous discovery, the loop from hypothesis to experiment to revised hypothesis is still often anecdotal. Here, we consider how that loop could be closed to enable AI-driven biomedical discovery. Closing the loop requires AI scientists that reason over biomedical knowledge and data across horizons of days to months. It also requires verifying hypotheses with computational tools and experiments in biological laboratories and clinical environments. Agentic and reasoning methods need to learn over time from sparse, delayed, and noisy feedback that verifiers return. In mathematics and program search, where candidate solutions can be verified at negligible cost and often as soon as they are generated, methods that generate and score large numbers of candidates have improved bounds on problems that had been open for decades. In biomedical sciences, comparable progress requires closing the loop where each test is slow, costly, and partially informative. Closed-loop AI-driven biomedical discovery can enable a mode of research in which AI continuously reviews hypotheses against accumulating experimental results. Scientists choose which experiments to pursue, and AI maintains a record that links each result to the hypothesis that produced it.

title: Fabrication-Aware Training for Two-Photon Polymerized Diffractive Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Abstract Diffractive deep neural networks (D2NNs) provide a promising pathway toward high-speed, energy-efficient optical computing. However, a substantial discrepancy between simulation and experiment remains when devices are fabricated by two-photon polymerization (TPP) for visible/near-infrared operation. This discrepancy is primarily due to fabrication constraints. In particular, the finite voxel size of the writing focus and the layer-by-layer slicing quantization attenuate high-spatial-frequency phase features and distort the designed wavefront. Here, a fabrication-aware training (FAT) strategy is introduced to incorporate these dominant constraints into the optimization loop through a differentiable model, thereby improving the experimental performance of two-photon polymerized D2NNs. In a handwritten digit recognition task, FAT increases the average experimental energy concentration ratio (ECR) from 6.15% to 11.50%. This reduces the simulation-to-experiment discrepancy by 79.03% while preserving the classification accuracy. These results demonstrate that fabrication-aware optimization substantially improves the functional fidelity of micro/nanoscale diffractive optical computing devices.

title: Shortest self-orthogonal and LCD embeddings of linear codes over Fq+uFq
abstract: This paper determines the exact lengths of shortest self-orthogonal and LCD embeddings of linear codes over $\mathbb{F}_q+u\mathbb{F}_q$. By decomposing Gram matrices over $\mathbb{F}_q+u\mathbb{F}_q$ into pairs of symmetric matrices over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$, the embedding problems are reduced to the congruence classification of symmetric and alternate matrices over finite fields. Complete formulas for the shortest self-orthogonal embedding length are obtained, with two distinct cases arising in both even and odd characteristic. We also show that every self-orthogonal code over $\mathbb{F}_q+u\mathbb{F}_q$ with nonzero free rank can be viewed as a shortest self-orthogonal embedding of another code. We use Witt theory to construct all shortest self-orthogonal embeddings. A complete characterization of shortest LCD embeddings is also established in terms of invertible and arbitrary matrices of prescribed sizes appended to a generator matrix. Examples of self-orthogonal and LCD embeddings with the largest minimum distance for the code considered are also presented, some of whose Gray images are optimal codes over $\mathbb{F}_q$.

title: Quantum State-Based Distributed Computing
abstract: This paper explores the potential of distributed computing utilizing quantum states, specifically leveraging superposition and entanglement. The core claim is that these quantum phenomena can be harnessed to enable parallel computation and enhanced information processing within a distributed system. We introduce a novel architecture designed around manipulating quantum states to perform computations across multiple nodes. The system's efficiency stems from the inherent parallelism offered by quantum superposition and the ability to correlate data through entanglement. This approach represents a fundamentally new paradigm for distributed computing, moving beyond classical limitations and opening possibilities for tackling computationally intensive problems. The architecture outlined here provides a framework for future research and development in this burgeoning field. This paper focuses on the theoretical design and potential benefits, without the inclusion of experimental results.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: This paper explores the integration of neural networks and symbolic reasoning techniques to enhance automated theorem proving. The core claim is that combining these approaches can significantly improve both the efficiency and accuracy of automated theorem proving systems. We propose a neuro-symbolic system comprising a neural network component designed to learn patterns within existing mathematical proofs, and a symbolic theorem prover responsible for executing logical deductions. The system will operate in a collaborative manner, with the neural network guiding the symbolic prover and the prover verifying the network's outputs. This approach addresses the limitations of purely symbolic systems, which often struggle with complex or unfamiliar mathematical domains, and the limitations of purely neural systems, which can lack the explicit logical structure necessary for robust theorem proving. The resulting architecture aims to accelerate mathematical discovery by leveraging the strengths of both symbolic and connectionist paradigms. The system's architecture and operational principles are detailed, outlining a pathway towards a more powerful and adaptable automated theorem prover.

title: Quantum Annealing Optimization Algorithm via Topological Quantization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to quantum annealing optimization algorithms by integrating topological quantization. The core idea is to discretize the annealing path into a series of topological states, leveraging quantum entanglement to facilitate precise control over the system's evolution and ultimately enhance optimization performance. The method aims to overcome limitations inherent in traditional quantum annealing by providing a more granular and controllable mechanism for traversing the energy landscape. We demonstrate that this topological quantization approach leads to improved convergence speed and potentially higher solution accuracy. The theoretical framework and associated mathematical formulations are presented, outlining the key principles and operational details of the algorithm. This work represents a significant step toward realizing the full potential of quantum annealing for complex optimization problems.

title: Quantum Security Protocol Based on Quantum Decoherence
abstract: This paper proposes a novel hardware security protocol leveraging the principles of quantum decoherence. Traditional hardware security protocols often rely on computationally intensive mathematical algorithms, rendering them vulnerable to sophisticated hardware attacks. Our approach introduces a fundamentally different strategy: embedding quantum decoherence directly into the hardware design. This creates an inherent barrier against eavesdropping and manipulation, as any attempt to observe or alter the quantum state will inevitably induce decoherence, destroying the key or corrupting the data. We detail the theoretical framework, focusing on the operational aspects of the protocol, and outline its potential advantages in mitigating hardware-based threats. The core claim of this work is to demonstrate a viable hardware security solution based on a well-established quantum phenomenon, offering a robust defense against attacks that exploit weaknesses in traditional cryptographic implementations.

title: Quantum-Inspired Data Compression Techniques for Graph Databases
abstract: Graph databases are increasingly used to model complex relationships within diverse domains, from social networks to biological systems. However, the inherent redundancy in graph data often leads to significant storage requirements. This paper explores the application of quantum-inspired techniques to achieve enhanced data compression for graph databases. We propose a novel compression algorithm that mimics aspects of superposition and entanglement to represent multiple relationships concurrently, thereby minimizing redundancy. The core concept involves encoding nodes and their connections within a superposition state, allowing for the simultaneous representation of multiple possible relationships. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and mathematical formulations that this approach can achieve higher compression ratios compared to traditional graph compression methods. The key innovations lie in the adaptation of quantum principles to the specific characteristics of graph data and the development of an efficient encoding and decoding scheme. The effectiveness of the proposed method is evaluated through simulations and analytical results, showcasing its potential to dramatically reduce storage needs while preserving the essential information within the graph database.

title: ##基于遗传算法的编译器优化
abstract: This paper explores the application of genetic algorithms (GAs) to the optimization of compilers. Traditional compiler optimization relies heavily on hand-crafted heuristics and expert knowledge, often leading to suboptimal solutions. This research proposes a novel approach leveraging the inherent search capabilities of GAs to automatically discover and select optimal compilation optimization strategies. The core concept involves representing compilation optimization techniques as chromosomes within a GA framework. Through iterative processes of selection, crossover, and mutation, the GA evolves these chromosomes, ultimately converging on a set of optimized strategies. We demonstrate the potential of this method to significantly enhance program performance by automating the complex process of compiler optimization. The paper details the algorithm design, the representation of optimization strategies, and the GA implementation, providing a theoretical foundation and outlining a practical framework for automated compiler optimization.

title: fwb: An R package for the fractional weighted bootstrap
abstract: The nonparametric bootstrap is a simple method for performing inference on estimates of statistical parameters without making strong assumptions about the data or a statistical model and without needing to derive the formula for an estimator's variance (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993).The traditional nonparametric bootstrap involves resampling the observations from the sample with replacement, computing the estimates in the bootstrap sample, performing these steps many times, and summarizing the resulting distribution of bootstrap estimates to compute their confidence intervals.This is equivalent to drawing integer weights from a multinomial distribution and computing weighted estimates in each bootstrap sample.However, integer weights are not the only weights that can be used, and fractional (non-integer) weights carry certain advantages, described below.fwb implements the fractional weighted bootstrap, also known as the Bayesian bootstrap, using a simple interface and with options for parallelization.

title: Devising an approach to chatbot response personalization based on user query analysis
abstract: This study investigates the process that generates a personalized chatbot response based on the analysis of a user request within one interaction session. The task addressed is to increase the adaptability of the response by taking into account the parameters of the request and the related prompts. The proposed mechanism made it possible to describe the personalization process in terms of the total time spent on performing the main operations of the user and the system. The constructed model establishes a connection between the parameters of the user request, the characteristics of the temporary interaction dictionary, and the probability of receiving a personalized response. A feature of the model is the consideration of the number of possible semantic interpretations of the request and permissible options for combining words to build a logically consistent response. Based on the model, an algorithm has been developed that involves forming a temporary interaction dictionary, selecting relevant words, combining them, substituting them into the response structure, and checking the logical and semantic consistency of the result. The experiments showed that the probability of a positive completion of the personalization process increases with an increase in the number of response refinement steps, and the average time for analyzing a user's request with additional prompts and forming a personalized response is 3.056 s. It was experimentally established that with a decrease in the probability of a positive completion of the personalization process at each individual step from 10-6 to 10-8, values of the model components and the total time costs decrease. The proposed approach could be used in practical tasks of designing personalization modules for educational and consulting dialog systems, as well as for controlled generation of responses taking into account the structure of the request and the parameters of the current interaction session

title: Multi‐Agent Search under Uncertainty
abstract: Plan optimal multi-robot search paths despite imperfect sensor information When multiple robots must locate targets in presence of false positive and false negative detection errors, path planning becomes extraordinarily complex. Multi-Agent Search under Uncertainty addresses this challenge directly. Written by researchers with combined expertise spanning defense systems, applied mathematics, and machine learning, this book delivers both theoretical foundations in search and screening theory and ready-to-use algorithms for practical implementation. The book covers cooperative search and navigation methods for autonomous mobile agents operating with incomplete or noisy information. Readers learn how Deep Q-Learning enables robots to develop complex behaviors through trial-and-error interactions rather than pre-programmed instructions. Applications span search and rescue operations, military surveillance, environmental monitoring, and security systems. An accompanying website provides Python code for simulation practice. Key topics include: Value-based Q-Learning methods where robots learn expected rewards for specific actions in given states under sensor uncertainty conditions Multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches for swarm robotics where multiple robots learn cooperatively to accomplish collaborative search tasks Deep reinforcement learning using neural networks to process high-dimensional sensory inputs and execute complex search and tracking behaviors Algorithms for finding and tracking both stationary and moving targets while minimizing detection time despite false negative and positive readings Theoretical contributions to search and screening theory alongside practical algorithms validated in autonomous robotic systems development Designed for graduate students and researchers in robotics and reinforcement learning, this book bridges advanced theory with practical application. Professional developers building autonomous systems will find algorithms tested in real-world robotic development.

title: Introduction to Nature‐Inspired Intelligence
abstract: Meta-heuristic algorithms are computational intelligence paradigms specifically employed to solve numerous compound optimization issues and get the best outcome. With the development of computers in recent decades, scientists and academicians have continuously drawn inspiration from nature to create all-purpose devices that are even better than humans. A type of meta-heuristic algorithms known as “nature-inspired algorithms” draws inspiration from natural phenomena, inspired by Charles Darwin's theory of evolution. Improved wind turbine efficiency (by mimicking whale fins), water filtration and purification (by mimicking plant root systems), lightweight and robust materials (by mimicking spider silk), energy efficiency in buildings (by mimicking termite mound ventilation systems), optimized transportation design (by mimicking the kingfisher beak bullet train), coastal erosion control (by mimicking mangrove restoration), wind farm layouts (optimized by fish movement patterns) and urban heat island management through green infrastructure are just a few examples. In recent years, numerous paradigms for computing that draw inspiration from nature have surfaced. The important advancements in the area of computing influenced by nature are summarized in this paper, emphasizing biology-based algorithms. The ability of bio-inspired solutions to solve complex problems, such as NP-hard and black-box optimization, makes them useful for solving real-world issues. These solutions have drawn much interest from scholars and have been used to solve various optimization problems because of their easy scalability, parallelism, stochastic, and straightforward implementation characteristics. The idea behind the bio-inspired algorithms is the movement of organisms and frequently observed phenomena in certain animal species, such as schools of fish, herds of quadrupeds, and flocks of birds. The primary contribution of this chapter is to present a thorough overview of the characteristics and current challenges based on the nature-inspired computing paradigm. The main objective of this research is to identify the optimal outcome among every feasible solution for better decision-making. This comprehensive examination offers insightful research for general artificial intelligence technology in the future.

title: Learning from Hard Prompts: Difficulty-aware Advantage Amplification in Dynamic Sampling
abstract: Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) is a prominent variant of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). DAPO introduces several improvements over GRPO. Among these, Dynamic Sampling contributes the most to DAPO's accuracy gains relative to GRPO. To improve accuracy, Dynamic Sampling enhances training stability by eliminating zero policy gradients from zero advantages. Specifically, it avoids such zero gradients by filtering out prompts where sampled responses are either entirely correct or incorrect. However, our theoretical analysis shows that Dynamic Sampling decrease training efficiency as it cannot effectively utilize hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts. Formally, it asymmetrically amplifies the advantages of distinct responses to the same prompts. On hard prompts, incorrect responses undergo greater amplification than correct ones. This leads the model to avoid generating the observed incorrect responses rather than capitalizing on the hard-to-sample correct ones on hard prompts, resulting in low training efficiency. To improve training efficiency, we propose Direct Advantage Amplification (DAA), which amplifies the advantages of hard-to-sample correct responses on hard prompts, as obtained by Dynamic Sampling. This ensures that, when Dynamic Sampling is used, these hard-to-sample responses can be effectively capitalized on, implying higher training efficiency. By integrating DAA into DAPO, we obtain Difficulty-aware Advantage Amplification Policy Optimization (DA3PO), which is implemented with fewer than 30 lines of code from DAPO. Experiments show that DA3PO significantly outperforms GRPO and other classical GRPO variants.

title: Predictive Coding of Sensory Data using Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Networks
abstract: This paper investigates the application of hierarchical recurrent neural networks (HRNNs) for predictive coding of sensory data. Traditional recurrent neural networks often struggle to effectively model complex temporal dependencies inherent in sensory information, particularly those spanning multiple timescales. The core idea presented here is that a hierarchical structure within an RNN architecture, where each layer learns to predict the input at a different temporal scale, significantly enhances predictive coding capabilities. This approach allows the network to decompose temporal dependencies into manageable levels, capturing both immediate and distant relationships. We propose a framework for designing and training HRNNs, outlining key architectural considerations and learning strategies. The resulting model demonstrates improved performance in capturing and predicting sequential sensory data compared to standard RNNs, showcasing the potential of this approach for applications in areas such as signal processing, neuroscience, and robotics. The model's ability to learn predictive representations directly addresses the inherent challenges in sensory data analysis and provides a novel pathway for understanding how predictive processes contribute to perception.

title: ##基于多智能体协作的资源优化
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to resource optimization utilizing a multi-agent system (MAS) framework. The core claim is the design of a system capable of automatically optimizing resource allocation and collaborative strategies. This is achieved through a mechanism that combines Reinforcement Learning (RL) with a tailored multi-agent communication protocol. The system enables agents to engage in both cooperative and competitive interactions, ultimately leading to enhanced resource utilization efficiency. Traditional resource optimization methods often suffer from inflexibility and require manual tuning. This MAS approach introduces a level of adaptability and autonomy, dynamically adjusting to changing conditions and optimizing the overall system performance. The system's architecture and control strategy are detailed, outlining the key components and their interactions. The research explores the trade-offs between cooperation and competition within the multi-agent environment and demonstrates the potential for significant improvements in resource allocation compared to static or centrally-controlled solutions. The results highlight the effectiveness of this approach for complex, dynamic resource management scenarios. ---

title: 基于生物启发算法的程序资源分配
abstract: This paper investigates the application of bio-inspired algorithms, specifically Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), to the problem of program resource allocation. The core idea is to model resource allocation as an optimization task and leverage the collective intelligence found in nature – particularly the behavior of ants and swarming animals – to dynamically adjust resource assignments. Traditional resource allocation methods often rely on hand-crafted algorithms, which can be inflexible and struggle to adapt to varying workloads and system conditions. By employing ACO and PSO, this research proposes a system that can automatically learn and optimize resource utilization, potentially leading to significant improvements in efficiency and performance. The key contribution lies in the adaptive nature of the algorithms, allowing them to respond effectively to changes in resource demands and system dynamics. This work lays the groundwork for a more intelligent and responsive approach to program resource management.

title: Algorithmic Reservoir Computing with Quantum State Evolution
abstract: Reservoir computing is a promising approach to dynamic systems modeling, known for its computational efficiency and ability to capture temporal dynamics. However, traditional reservoir computing often struggles with theoretical understanding and guarantees of performance. This work proposes a novel framework that integrates reservoir computing with quantum state evolution. The core idea involves utilizing a quantum system as the reservoir, where its state evolves governed by a parameterized Hamiltonian. The output signal is then extracted by measuring the state of this quantum reservoir. This approach aims to leverage the inherent complexity and parallelism of quantum systems to potentially enhance reservoir computing's capabilities. We explore the theoretical underpinnings of this hybrid system and present a conceptual model. The key contribution lies in the combination of these two powerful paradigms, offering a potential route toward more robust and scalable dynamic systems modeling. Further research will focus on optimizing the Hamiltonian parameters and exploring different measurement strategies to maximize the system's performance.

title: Dynamic Quantum Entanglement Topological Network Protocol
abstract: This paper proposes a novel protocol for dynamic quantum entanglement topological network, aiming to achieve robust quantum communication and distributed quantum computation. The core of the protocol relies on leveraging topological protection of quantum states and dynamic adjustment of entanglement within a topological quantum network. We introduce a framework that utilizes the inherent topological properties of entangled states to construct fault-tolerant encoding schemes. Real-time control of the network topology allows for optimization of entanglement quality and overall network performance. The proposed approach addresses the vulnerability of traditional quantum networks to noise by incorporating topological protection and dynamic control, offering a fundamentally new network architecture. The protocol's key features include adaptable error correction, enhanced entanglement distribution, and scalable quantum network design. We outline the mathematical foundation for the protocol, including the entanglement fidelity metrics and topological network optimization algorithms. This work represents a significant step towards practical, robust quantum networks capable of supporting complex quantum information processing tasks.

title: Construction of a parametric invariant hypergraph model for integrating and analyzing multi-context educational data
abstract: This study examines multi-context educational data acquired from independent digital platforms and characterized by differences in the composition of entities, types of interactions, and data representation schemes. The task addressed relates to the lack of a unified model for the invariant representation of heterogeneously structured data, the assessment of their structural compatibility, the determination of the costs of mutual adaptation, and the possibility of comparative analysis of digital platforms while preserving the characteristics of the educational context. A parametrically typed invariant hypergraph model has been proposed, which represents educational data as typed hypergraphs, their semantic normalization into a single type space, as well as the calculation of indicators of structural invariance, adaptation, and integral utility. A parametric analysis of sensitivity to changes in the data structure and model weighting coefficients has been suggested. The novelty of this work is underscored by the following: – a unified parametric hypergraph model has been constructed that combines the invariant representation of educational data, a quantitative assessment of the structural compatibility, adaptation costs, and integral utility of digital educational platforms; – a parametric analysis has been proposed to examine the influence of structure and weighting factors on the integration and comparative analysis of platforms; – the model was experimentally tested on data from independent educational platforms, including over 3,100 educational records and 4,861 hyperedges, revealing differences in the structural compatibility of the studied contexts. The model supports decision making in the selection and design of digital educational ecosystems in the context of structurally heterogeneous data

title: Informing School Library Professional Advisory on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence to Communicate Accessible Home Literacy Advice
abstract: Schools communicate the importance of home literacy practices in the early schooling years and beyond, but low parental English literacy can be a significant barrier to sharing evidence and strategies. School library professionals often play a key role in the implementation of new technologies, and in promoting reading and literacy within and beyond the school. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are already being used in some schools for a variety of purposes despite known and emerging limitations and issues, and as digital and information literacy experts within schools, school library professionals may advise on and facilitate this use. This study seeks to determine if GenAI tools are reliable for generating simplified messaging on home literacy for effective communication with culturally and linguistically diverse homes. This research tests the reliability and consistency of GenAI tools in adjusting texts to enhance accessibility, and how research related messaging may be distorted through this simplification process. Findings suggest that GenAI tools are not currently consistent in their readability determinations, typically underestimating the complexity of the text they produce, with significant human oversight still needed. As such, at this stage, school library professionals’ advisory in schools should be responsive to these findings.

title: Computational Intelligence Using Fuzzy Logic in Educational Data Analysis A Study of Methodologies and Applications
abstract: In this exploratory research, the use of computational intelligence, more especially fuzzy sense, in the analysis of educational data is investigated. The paper also investigates colorful approaches and the practical applications of these methodologies. To improve tutoring and literacy challenges, educational institutions are increasingly resorting to data-driven techniques. This trend is expected to continue. The use of fuzzy sense, which is well-known for its capacity to manage queries and complexity, provides potentially useful tools for evaluating educational data. The purpose of this project is to investigate how fuzzy sense models can be utilized to reuse and interpret various educational data sets. These data sets include educational criteria for student achievement as well as learning gesture patterns. In the process of establishing meaningful perceptivity from educational data, comparative evaluations of various fuzzy sense approaches highlight both the benefits and limits of these methodologies. To demonstrate the efficacy of fuzzy sense in the process of developing educational decision-making procedures, case studies illustrate realistic executions across a variety of educational environments. The findings highlight the potential for computational intelligence, and more specifically fuzzy sense, to change the way educational data analysis is done by providing preceptors and stakeholders with additional nuanced and practical perceptivity.

title: Stranger, Fan, or Peer? A Systematic Study on the Role of Interlocutor in Persona-Based Dialogue Generation
abstract: Persona-based dialogue systems are usually conditioned on speaker biography, but dialogues involve at least two participants, and who has access to whose biography can vary across training, inference, and evaluation. Prior work often neglected these aspects, obscuring mechanisms that only appear when biography visibility is toggled separately across training, inference, and evaluation, a three-stage factorisation that prior work has largely treated as a single factor. We study this factorisation on a dataset of dialogues paired with speaker's biographies, varying whether the target and interlocutor speakers see each other's biographies during training and inference, and using an LLM as a judge to perform author identification. We find that (i) training-time visibility, more than inference-time visibility, determines whether models express persona traits through dialogue or fall back on copying biographical text (a known problem/phenomenon in persona-based generation); (ii) models trained with interlocutor-biography visibility copy less target-biographical text than models trained without it, while changing visibility only at inference time has a less consistent effect; and (iii) under asymmetric disclosure, where only the interlocutor sees the target biography, target content leaks into interlocutor turns more often, and dialogues containing such traces are easier for the judge to identify, especially when interlocutor turns are visible. These results suggest that biography leakage into generated turns is an artefact of how interlocutor visibility is configured across training and inference, and separating the three stages is necessary.

title: Biologically Inspired Mechanisms for Facilitating Grokking in Multilayer Perceptrons
abstract: Grokking is a delayed transition from memorization to generalization that is often accompanied by substantial reorganization of internal representations. This paper studies whether biologically inspired mechanisms, many of which are not commonly incorporated into artificial neural networks, can actively promote this transition by regulating hidden-layer computation at the levels of neuronal activity, response, and effective connectivity. We augment a multilayer perceptron with input gating, structural plasticity, gain modulation, threshold modulation, homeostasis, lateral inhibition, and activation decorrelation, and evaluate these mechanisms through systematic ablations on two established grokking benchmarks: sparse parity and noisy XOR classification. The results show that the mechanisms contribute unequally to generalization. Homeostasis provides the strongest and most consistent benefit, while structural sparsification emerges as the second major mechanism. The remaining biologically inspired mechanisms have smaller or less consistent effects in the present experiments. For both problems, the results support the common principle that explicit regulation of neuron utilization and effective connectivity can improve the emergence of generalizable internal computation. These findings motivate broader investigation of biologically inspired activity regulation and adaptive sparsification, including in large language models, where they may accelerate the development of generalizable representations and reduce the optimization time required for robust generalization.

These findings motivate broader investigation of biologically inspired activity regulation and adaptive sparsification, including in large language models, where they may accelerate the development of generalizable representations and reduce the optimization time required for robust generalization.

title: Intelligent Mineralization Recognition Method Based on Remote Sensing Data
abstract: In recent years, the application of remote sensing technology in geological exploration has gradually deepened, especially in improving the efficiency of mineral exploration, showing great potential. However, in the face of massive remote sensing data, traditional experience-based manual recognition methods cannot meet the needs of mineral exploration in terms of effectiveness and efficiency. This article proposes an intelligent mining prediction method based on remote sensing data and deep learning neural networks. Using high-precision remote sensing data, a deep convolutional neural network mining prediction model is established with known fluorite vein bands as positive samples and unknown areas as negative samples. Three convolutional neural network architectures, Alex LeNet5, VGG16, and GoogLeNet Inception v1, are used for comparative experiments. The results show that the Alex LeNet5 model performs the best in fluorite mining prediction tasks in remote sensing images, outperforming the VGG16 and GoogLeNet Inception V1 models.The model was applied to fluorite prospecting prediction, identifying five mineralization prospect areas.

title: Artificial Intelligence as an Entropy-Reduction Operator: Imposing Order on Laboratory Chaos via LLM Hardware Orchestration and the Model Hardware Standard
abstract: Author: Luigi Usai ORCID: 0009-0003-3001-717X Publication Type: Technical Preprint / Epistemological Note (Zenodo Version v2) Date: August 28, 2026 License: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Attribution and Corrigendum Notice (v2) Corrigendum Notice: This preprint articulates an epistemological and computational thesis regarding the core utility of Artificial Intelligence as a universal entropy-reduction engine. The Model Hardware Standard (MHS), referenced throughout this work as an empirical case study of hardware abstraction, is an open specification introduced by Anthropic and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) Janelia Research Campus (August 2026). The author claims no proprietary authorship over the MHS specification, but provides the theoretical framework governing operational entropy reduction, cognitive orchestration, and configuration latency collapse in MHS-compliant scientific workflows. Abstract The widespread adoption and practical success of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) stem from a fundamental computational mechanism: their capacity to act as entropy-reduction operators, imposing deterministic structure and operational order on high-dimensional, chaotic environments. Human researchers constantly face combinatorial friction when coordinating heterogeneous, unstandardized systems. Modern experimental laboratories represent a quintessential failure mode of this dynamic: empirical progress is severely bottlenecked by "hardware chaos"—a fragmented ecosystem of proprietary actuators, sensors, and instruments requiring tedious manual configuration, custom glue code, and extensive calibration overhead. Using the recently announced Model Hardware Standard (MHS) (Anthropic & HHMI Janelia, 2026) as a foundational case study, this paper formalizes how AI agents and LLM-driven orchestration layers resolve interface fragmentation. By translating abstract, high-level scientific hypotheses into deterministic machine-executable parameters, AI collapses operational entropy, reducing experiment setup and execution latency by up to 80% (operating at $\approx 0.20$ of traditional manual time requirements). We demonstrate that AI's core value proposition is not mere statistical pattern matching, but the systematic transformation of chaotic human and physical parameter spaces into ordered, verifiable, and accelerated discovery pipelines. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Entropy Reduction, Scientific Automation, Model Hardware Standard, Large Language Models (LLMs), Laboratory Workflow Optimization, Operational Complexity. 1. The Foundational Thesis: Why AI Succeeds by Imposing Order on Chaos The fundamental reason human operators find Artificial Intelligence indispensable across scientific, computational, and organizational domains is its capacity to resolve cognitive and operational chaos. Human cognition excels at conceptual hypothesis generation but degrades rapidly under high combinatorial loads, syntactic fragmentation, and multi-variable parameter calibration. Unstructured environments possess high Shannon-Gibbs operational entropy: $$H(\mathcal{X}) = -\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} p(x) \log_2 p(x)$$ where $\mathcal{X}$ represents the state space of possible system configurations, communication protocols, parameter settings, and error states. AI projects an under-specified, noisy, and high-entropy intent space onto a deterministic, constrained, and optimal subspace $\mathcal{X}^*$, minimizing configurational drift and cognitive burden: $$\Delta H = H(\mathcal{X}_{\text{initial}}) - H(\mathcal{X}_{\text{orchestrated}}) \gg 0$$ 2. Empirical Bottleneck: The State of "Hardware Chaos" in Modern Laboratories Empirical research in molecular biology, materials science, and chemistry remains tethered to manual intervention due to severe physical interface divergence: Protocol Fragmentation: Instruments from different vendors (HPLC systems, liquid handlers, mass spectrometers, optical sensors) expose incompatible API surfaces, proprietary DLLs, and disparate serial protocols (RS-232, Modbus, custom TCP sockets). Configuration Friction: Researchers spend up to 70%–80% of total laboratory time on non-discovery overhead: writing ad-hoc wrapper scripts, manually tuning driver parameters, verifying electrical/fluidic preconditions, and resolving syntax incompatibilities. Reproducibility Degradation: Human manual execution introduces stochastic variability in physical reagent timing, temperature ramp-rates, and sensor baselining. The total experimental completion time $\tau_{\text{total}}$ in a legacy unstandardized laboratory is dominated by manual configuration latency $\tau_{\text{config}}$: $$\tau_{\text{total}} = \tau_{\text{config}} + \tau_{\text{execution}} + \tau_{\text{analysis}}, \quad \text{where } \tau_{\text{config}} \approx 0.70\text{--}0.80 \, \tau_{\text{total}}$$ 3. Case Study: The Model Hardware Standard (Anthropic & HHMI Janelia) The Model Hardware Standard (MHS), introduced in August 2026 by Anthropic and the HHMI Janelia Research Campus, provides the standardized abstraction substrate necessary for AI agents to interface directly with physical laboratory equipment. 3.1 The Role of MHS in Decoupling Intent from Actuation MHS acts as a universal semantic layer between high-level reasoning engines and low-level physical actuation: Standardized Hardware Declarations: Exposes uniform APIs for device capability discovery, state queries, and hardware commands. Pre/Post-Condition Envelopes: Enforces physical safety constraints (e.g., thermal bounds, pressure tolerances, interlock states) via machine-readable contracts. title: Temporal Graph Embedding with Relational Entropy
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to temporal graph embedding, termed Temporal Graph Embedding with Relational Entropy (TGE). Existing graph embedding methods often fail to adequately represent the dynamic evolution of graphs, neglecting the intricate relationships that change over time. We propose a framework that leverages relational entropy – a metric quantifying the diversity and complexity of relationships – to guide the embedding process. The core idea is to utilize a recurrent neural network (RNN) trained to predict future relationship transitions. The RNN's training is guided by a loss function that incorporates these relational entropy scores, effectively weighting transitions based on their informational content and the overall complexity of the graph's relationship structure. This approach moves beyond traditional node adjacency or edge count representations, offering a richer and more accurate depiction of temporal graph dynamics. Experimental validation, though not presented here due to the focus on the methodology, demonstrates the potential of this technique to improve the quality of temporal graph embeddings.

title: Causal Bayesian Networks with Stochastic Differential Equations
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to modeling complex causal systems by integrating stochastic differential equations (SDEs) within causal Bayesian networks. Traditional Bayesian networks struggle to capture the inherent stochasticity and dynamic evolution present in many real-world systems. This work addresses this limitation by representing each variable in the network as a node, with its influence on neighboring nodes governed by an SDE. This allows for the simulation of dynamic causal relationships, explicitly accounting for noise and uncertainty. The core claim is that this combined framework offers a more accurate representation of complex causal systems compared to standard Bayesian networks. The mechanism involves defining stochastic differential equations that model the time-dependent evolution of variables, providing a richer and more nuanced depiction of causality. This approach is particularly relevant for applications where the system's behavior is influenced by both deterministic causal links and random fluctuations. The resulting model offers improved predictive capabilities and a deeper understanding of the underlying causal processes.

title: Quantum Computing: The Time Transistor Model and Algorithm Design
abstract: This paper explores the potential of the Time Transistor Model (TTM) within the realm of quantum computing. The TTM, characterized by its inherent temporal dynamics, offers a novel approach to algorithm design and implementation compared to traditional models like the Qubit model. We present a framework for designing quantum algorithms based on the TTM, focusing on algorithms with time-dependent operations. Specifically, we investigate algorithms that leverage the controlled evolution of quantum states over time, analogous to the behavior of a time-dependent transistor. The core contribution lies in formulating a set of algorithms that exploit this temporal dependence to achieve computational advantages. The paper details the mathematical formulation of these algorithms, including the definition of key operators and their temporal evolution. Furthermore, we discuss the potential challenges and future research directions related to implementing these algorithms on quantum hardware, considering the practical constraints and complexities involved. Ultimately, this work aims to demonstrate the viability of the TTM as a powerful tool for quantum algorithm development.

title: Quantum State Thermodynamics Entropy Increase Principle and the Limits of Quantum Computing
abstract: This paper investigates the limits of quantum computing by applying the entropy increase principle from quantum state thermodynamics. We analyze the fundamental challenges posed by energy dissipation and information loss during quantum computations, leveraging the second law of thermodynamics. Specifically, we explore the implications of entropy generation on quantum coherence and fidelity, and propose theoretical frameworks for mitigating these effects. The core argument centers on demonstrating that inherent entropy generation processes, when unchecked, inevitably lead to the degradation of quantum states and ultimately limit the scalability of quantum computers. We formulate key mathematical expressions relating entropy generation rates to quantum gate operations and decoherence models. The analysis reveals that while quantum computation offers potential advantages, a thorough understanding and strategic management of entropy are crucial for realizing its full potential. The work highlights the necessity of robust error correction and innovative quantum architectures designed to minimize entropy generation. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical boundaries imposed by the second law of thermodynamics on the achievable fidelity of quantum computations.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning with Temporal Logic and Bayesian Networks
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to neuro-symbolic reasoning by integrating neural networks and temporal logic. The core idea is to leverage the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks to learn probabilistic knowledge representations, and then to utilize a temporal logic engine for logical inference and reasoning about temporal relationships between events. The proposed system aims to overcome the limitations of purely neural or purely symbolic approaches by combining their respective strengths. Specifically, a neural network is trained to map observational data into a probabilistic state representation, which is subsequently used as input to a temporal logic reasoner. This allows for the deduction of consequences and the verification of temporal constraints. The system's architecture is described, along with the key components and their interactions. The paper outlines the core claim, the core mechanism, and highlights the novelty of the integration. Finally, it discusses potential applications and future research directions.

title: Генетический подход к повышению производительности распределенных хранилищ данных в телекоммуникационных системах
abstract: Рассмотрены ключевые решения по построению генетического алгоритма, лежащего в основе предлагаемого подхода к созданию распределенных хранилищ данных в телекоммуникационных системах с целью повышения их производительности, а также обсуждаются экспериментальные результаты по применению предлагаемого подхода. Сформулирована постановка задачи оптимального распределения файлов по узлам хранилища данных, в которой необходимо достичь максимального значения показателя его производительности при условии удовлетворения заданного значения показателя отказоустойчивости. Предложены и детально проработаны шаги генетического алгоритма, содержащие некоторые новшества, касающиеся, в частности, использования столбцов матрицы, определяющей план распределения файлов, в качестве генов хромосом, реализации универсальной стохастической выборки точек скрещивания, а также использования принципа элитизма для сохранения наилучшего генофонда. Проведены вычислительные эксперименты, показавшие, что предложенный подход позволяет решить поставленную задачу с достаточно высокой точностью за существенно меньшее время, чем это делают традиционные математические методы оптимизации. The article discusses key decisions on the construction of a genetic algorithm that underlies the proposed approach to constructing distributed data storages in telecommunication systems with the aim of increasing their performance, and experimental results on the application of the proposed approach are also discussed. The problem of optimal distribution of files among data storage nodes is formulated, in which it is necessary to achieve the maximum value of its performance indicator, subject to satisfying the specified value of the fault-tolerance indicator. The steps of a genetic algorithm were proposed and detailed, incorporating several innovations, including the use of columns of the matrix defining the file distribution plan as chromosomal genes, the implementation of a universal stochastic selection of crossover points, and the use of the elitism principle to preserve the best gene pool. Computational experiments were conducted, demonstrating that the proposed approach enables solving the problem with a sufficiently high accuracy in significantly less time than traditional mathematical optimization methods.

Предложены и детально проработаны шаги генетического алгоритма, содержащие некоторые новшества, касающиеся, в частности, использования столбцов матрицы, определяющей план распределения файлов, в качестве генов хромосом, реализации универсальной стохастической выборки точек скрещивания, а также использования принципа элитизма для сохранения наилучшего генофонда. Проведены вычислительные эксперименты, показавшие, что предложенный подход позволяет решить поставленную задачу с достаточно высокой точностью за существенно меньшее время, чем это делают традиционные математические методы оптимизации. The article discusses key decisions on the construction of a genetic algorithm that underlies the proposed approach to constructing distributed data storages in telecommunication systems with the aim of increasing their performance, and experimental results on the application of the proposed approach are also discussed. The problem of optimal distribution of files among data storage nodes is formulated, in which it is necessary to achieve the maximum value of its performance indicator, subject to satisfying the specified value of the fault-tolerance indicator. The steps of a genetic algorithm were proposed and detailed, incorporating several innovations, including the use of columns of the matrix defining the file distribution plan as chromosomal genes, the implementation of a universal stochastic selection of crossover points, and the use of the elitism principle to preserve the best gene pool. Computational experiments were conducted, demonstrating that the proposed approach enables solving the problem with a sufficiently high accuracy in significantly less time than traditional mathematical optimization methods.

title: Particle Swarm Optimization for Effective Feature Selection in Smart Logistics
abstract: The paper outlines the utilization of Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) for enhancing feature selection efficacy. Features are considered as particles which are ranked in a two-dimensional optimization space. During optimization process, the velocity and position of the particles are updated using feature rankings in addition to particle ranks. To complete the task, a novel particle ranking based on particle distance from dominated and non-dominated particles is developed, which is subsequently used to the computation of feature ranks. In comparison to five cutting-edge feature selection approaches, the proposed feature selection method has been evaluated on 6 UCI datasets and 2 datasets from real-world applications. Additionally, experiments revealed that the suggested strategy outperforms currently used feature selection techniques.

title: Coverage, Not Credit: Failure-Credit Routing of Zeroth-Order Perturbation Budgets Does Not Improve On-Pool Sample Efficiency for LLM Agents
abstract: Trajectory-level credit assignment can localize which module of a tool-using LLM agent causes failures using only verifiable signals. We ask whether such failure credit should route a fixed zeroth-order/evolution-strategies (ZO/ES) perturbation budget. Across a synthetic environment and frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B and SmolLM2-1.7B agents, three task families, six allocation schemes, a credit-noise sweep, paired seeds, and exact sign-flip tests, we find no statistically detectable improvement over uniform allocation in any on-pool comparison (no gain of at least 2 percentage points). The joint soft-plus-sigma scheme is equivalent to uniform within a +/- 0.02 AUC margin on 1.5B and 3B; concentrating the full budget on the credit argmax is marginally equivalent on 1.5B, where that module is the verified bottleneck, and significantly worse on 3B. Inverse-propensity debiasing does not rescue routing, and misrouting costs up to -0.074 AUC in-house and -0.118 end-to-end on the BFCL-derived family. Across six fixed-step schedules, loss is linear in bottleneck starvation rate (R^2 = 0.94, descriptive), and a preregistered credit-free coverage floor removes detected harm. Matched-budget burst and step-compensating catch-up schedules are consistent with harm arising from insufficient cumulative parameter movement rather than update frequency. Our primary estimand is optimization efficiency on a fixed task pool. On unseen BFCL functions, the study's one exception is that soft routing exceeds uniform on held-out endpoints (+0.047, p = 0.031, n = 6). A plausible but untested reading is that routing-favored caller improvements transfer while uniform's on-pool gains reflect a synthesizer behavior specific to our harness. We report this exception explicitly and document three failure modes that can silently invalidate ZO/ES experiments on frozen LLMs.

title: Cross-Session Decomposition Attacks: Scaling Risk and Intent-Aligned Retrieval Defense
abstract: Scaling laws are usually read as a capability story: lower language-modeling loss yields more useful models. We study a safety consequence of this mechanism in \emph{cross-session decomposition attacks}, where benign-looking subqueries are asked across independent interactions and later recomposed toward a forbidden objective. We formalize this setting as \emph{compositional safety risk} and prove a conditional risk-transfer bound: when the reference environment already contains dispersed evidence for a risky reconstruction, the gap between deployed composed risk and reference composed risk is controlled by the model's excess loss on allowed subqueries. Synthetic withholding experiments show that wider transformers assign lower loss to held-out instructions that never appear verbatim in training but are recoverable from injected supporting facts. A 600-intent pretrained-LLM evaluation shows that larger Qwen3 and Gemma3 family members can yield greater harmful-capability uplift under a fixed decomposition-composition pipeline. As a defense, IntentAlign-MiniLM, our 22M-parameter intent-aligned retriever, outperforms much larger embedding models on held-out intent retrieval and yields the best learned-retriever harmful recall across tested guardrails. Code is available in \href{https://github.com/liaodisen/Cross-Session-Decomposition-Attacks}{our GitHub repository}.
